Posted August 24, 2007

Analysis by Richard Cowan



 

While Marijuana News was on hiatus there have been a number of interesting developments.

On the negative side, the UK has fallen into a truly bizarre fit of reefer madness, quite literally.

See

Cannabis smokers need to be locked up By Simon Heffer

 

After decades of reading prohibitionist screeds, I have to say that this is over the top, just amazingly obtuse and vicious. Heffer seems intent on proving John Stuart Mill right when he said, Conservatives are not necessarily stupid, but most stupid people are conservatives. Of course, he never met Michael Moore.

See

Sicko and The Return of MarijuanaNews.com. The Failure of the Left to Address the Drug War. By Richard Cowan.

 

 

In 2004, the UK reclassified cannabis in order to lessen the burden on the police.

See

Beyond Bonkers: UK "Reclassification" Of Cannabis Caps Weeks of Absurdity. Prime Minister Has A Drug Problem?

 

 

It seemed to have worked. Martin Barnes, chief executive of the UK charity DrugScope, was quoted as saying: "The fact that cannabis use has continued to fall to its lowest level in nearly 10 years is further evidence that the decision to reclassify the drug to class C was sound.  Some warned that the change would lead to an increase in cannabis use yet the reverse has happened, possibly because there is more awareness of the possible harms.  The fact that cannabis has been linked with triggering mental conditions could have changed people's attitude towards the drug.  Another possible explanation is the rise in binge drinking, which some people may be doing instead of taking cannabis."

 

 

But the prohibitionists are pushing for a reversal.
See

DrugScope disappointed as cannabis classification in doubt again

I think that these events prove that it will not be possible to have social peace while the drug warriors dominate the media.

From 1998 see
Marijuana Prohibition, Media Criticism, Copyrights and the 8th and 9th Commandments.

and from 2002,
especially

Negligent Journalism: Reader Beware or A Right to Expect More? The Drug Czar Says He Is Subject to the Scrutiny of the Press. The Significance of the Ultimate Lies. Analysis by Richard Cowan

 

 

In due course, I hope to have to be able to hold my nose and write a complete analysis of the UKs sad exercise in intellectual self-degradation, but in the meantime, I would like revisit another point highlighted by the reference to binge drinking, comparing the risks of cannabis and alcohol.

 

 

This is not a new subject for readers of MarijuanaNews.

See

Australian Prohibitionists Find It "Disturbing" that People Think Marijuana Less Dangerous Than Alcohol For Drivers. The Party Line More Important than Safe Driving.

and

Canada's Crime Rate Dropped In 1999 For 8th Consecutive Year Without Creating A Police State. But Marijuana Arrests Continue to Climb. Alcohol Related Violence Soars in UK. Lessons for Everyone.

and

Great London Times Column and News From New Zealand Compare Marijuana and Alcohol

 

SAFERCHOICE.org

However, a relatively new

Denver based organization, SaferChoice.org, has picked up this line of argument and has made the most of it, both in their home state and on campuses around the country. Inasmuch as cannabis is demonstrably Safer, i.e., less dangerous than alcohol, it should at the very least be subject to comparable rules and regulations.

See

No Medicine Is Smoked. Okay, But Why Isnt Cannabis Sold Over-the-Counter? New MAPS/NORML Vaporizer Study Undermines Key Part Of Prohibitionist Party Line On Smoked-Marijuana.

 

 

Consider the following excerpts from reports from the UK, just this year. Notice that the first three are from the Telegraph.

24-hour drinking casualties 'trebled'

By Rebecca Smithm, Medical Editor

Last Updated: 11:09am BST 19/07/2007

Violent crime up 5pc in UK

 

 

The law allowing 24-hour drinking has caused a three-fold rise in the number of people admitted to accident and emergency units with alcohol-related problems, doctors said today. 

 

 

Alcohol-related admissions to accident and emergency have risen since the extended licensing laws came into effect in November 2005

 

 

The medical research, published today in the journal Emergency Medicine, found there an increase in alcohol-related assaults, injuries and hospital admissions in March 2006 compared with the same month the previous year.

 

 

The proportion of alcohol-related attendances rose from 2.9 per cent in March 2005 to eight per cent in March 2006.

 

 

Alcohol-related assaults more than doubled from 27 to 62 and injuries connected to drinking almost trebled 44 to 129.

 

 

The number of patients who had to be admitted on to the wards rose from 24 to 71.

 

 

Treating alcohol-related injuries and diseases is estimated to cost the NHS £1.7 billion a year and it is thought drinking-related crime and disorder costs £7.3 billion.

 

 

The report said: "There are around 23,000 incidents of alcohol-related violence every week in the UK.

 

 

"In addition to violence-related injuries, alcohol represents a major burden for UK health services in general, and in emergency departments in particular."

Prof Ian Gilmore, president of the RoyalCollege of Physicians, said the study may have under-estimated the alcohol-related cases but the fact that there has been a threefold rise since the law was changed was "concerning".

Female secretaries 'at risk from alcohol'

By Rebecca Smith, Medical Editor

Last Updated: 6:13pm BST 23/08/2007

 

Female office juniors are almost twice as likely to die from drinking too much than the rest of the population, new figures have revealed.

 

 

There were 16,666 alcohol related deaths from 2001 to 2005... 

 

 

An analysis of deaths caused by alcohol has uncovered the professions most at risk of drinking themselves into an early grave

Men and women who work around drink such as bar staff, publicans, catering staff are most at risk, according to the Office of National Statistics.

 

 

Actresses are 1.8 times as likely to die from alcohol than the general population, followed by women who work as hairdressers who are at 1.4 times the general risk.

The figures also found that seafarers in the merchant navy were twice as likely to die from alcohol related causes such as cirrhosis, poisoning and pancreatitis.

 

 

Male middle-ranking civil servants were 1.9 times more likely to die that way than average, male musicians were 1.6 times more likely, male floorers and wall tilers were 1.6 times more likely and men working in security such as bouncers and bailiffs were 1.7 times more likely.

 

 

Some male members of the armed forces - such as sergeants and lower ranks in the Army and chief petty officers and lower ranks in the Navy - were 1.4 times more likely to die from an alcohol-related problem.

 

 

A spokeswoman for the ONS said it was 'startling how little the pattern had changed over the last 100 years.

 

 

The data show there were 16,666 alcohol related deaths from 2001 to 2005.

 

 

Figures released earlier this year found that deaths specifically due to alcohol have doubled in the last ten years.

 

Some estimates have put the true figure much higher at 22,000 deaths a year.

'The brutal fact is that Dominic looks like this because he was so drunk while in the womb'

By Olga Craig, Sunday Telegraph

Last Updated: 11:41pm BST 21/04/2007

 

 

More babies - one in 100 - are born with foetal alcohol syndrome than all the major genetic disorders combined, yet the public know almost nothing about it.

 

 

Dominic is one of the one in 100 British children born with Foetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD), the umbrella term for a range of disorders caused by a mother drinking alcohol while pregnant.

 

 

With 750,000 live births each year in this country, it is a condition that affects 7,500 children annually - more than the combined number of babies born with muscular dystrophy, spina bifida, HIV and Down's syndrome.

 

 

It is believed that up to three in every 1,000 babies suffer from the most severe form of the syndrome, which leads to brain damage and severe learning difficulties.

 

 

About 28 babies with the most severe form are born each week. Yet the woeful lack of diagnostic expertise within the medical profession and the lack of publicity given to the syndrome means that thousands of women drink, and drink heavily, during pregnancy, oblivious to the risk to their unborn child

 

 

The backbench bill, which is backed by the National Organisation for Foetal Alcohol Syndrome (NOFAS), gained an unopposed second reading. But it may face a rocky ride through the Commons, since many MPs believe it is yet another example of a nannying state. Without Government backing it is unlikely to become law.

As Britain's binge-drinking culture becomes ingrained in our psyche, all too few pregnant women are aware of the enormous risks to which they expose their unborn child if they continue to drink.

 

 

A recent study indicated that 61 per cent of women don't cut down at all, and a survey carried out by St George's hospital in London revealed that just under 50 per cent of mothers visiting the teenage antenatal clinic drank more than four units on a single occasion and 27 per cent admitted to at times "getting drunk".

 

 

In Britain, teenage drinking is much more widespread among girls than boys, with almost 30 per cent of under 20-year-olds confessing to drinking to excess at least three times a month, despite the £20 billion the Government's Alcohol Harm Reduction Strategy has thrown at the problem.  

By MARIA CHENG, AP Medical Writer

August 7, 2007

 

 

"There's been a frightening increase in alcoholic liver disease in recent years," said Dr. Ian Gilmore, president of the RoyalCollege of Physicians.

Deaths from cirrhosis in Britain increased dramatically over the past two decades, while they fell steadily everywhere else in the Western world, according to government statistics.

Attempts to curb binge drinking, including 2005 legislation allowing round the clock alcohol sales, might have worsened the situation. At one London hospital, doctors noticed that since the alcohol licensing law changed, alcohol-related overnight trips to emergency rooms tripled. The law's effect, however, has been limited because most pubs did not to apply for an all-night license.


In the past decade, hospital admissions across Britain related to excessive drinking doubled. In 1995-1996, 89,000 people were admitted for alcohol-related conditions; by 2005-2006, the figure was 187,000 people.


And unlike the most of the rest of Europe, Britons are drinking more every year.


Total alcohol consumption in Britain doubled between 1960 and 2004, from about 1.5 gallons per person over 14 years old to 3 gallons per person. In contrast, other European countries, particularly in the south, recorded drops in consumption.

So far today, there have been ZERO media calls about a new Canadian study that deals with the comparative risks of cannabis and alcohol.


 

Now being ignored by the media:

From NORML's Weekly News Bulletin - August 23, 2007

Alcohol And Cocaine But Not Cannabis Linked To Violent Behavior, Study Says

August 23, 2007 - Victoria, BC, Canada

Victoria, British Columbia: Cannabis use is not independently associated with causing violence, according to the results of a multivariate analysis to be published in the journal Addictive Behaviors.

 

 

Investigators at the University of Victoria, Centre for Addictions Research assessed how frequently subjects in a substance abuse treatment facility reported using cocaine, alcohol, and/or cannabis in the hours immediately prior to committing a violent act. Researchers also evaluated subjects personality for characteristics associated with violent behavior, such as risk-taking, impulsivity, and/or disrespect for the law.

 

 

Investigators concluded: "When analyses were conducted controlling for covariates, the frequency of alcohol and cocaine use was significantly related to violence, suggesting that pharmacological effects [of the drugs] may play a role in violence. Frequency of cannabis use, however, was not significantly related to violence when controlling for other factors."

The studys conclusions are similar to the findings of a pair of recent government reports refuting allegations that cannabis use triggers violent behavior. The first, published by the Canadian Senate in 2002, determined: "Cannabis use does not induce users to commit other forms of crime. Cannabis use does not increase aggressiveness or anti-social behavior."

 

 

The second review, published by the British Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs, reported: "Cannabis differs from alcohol in one major respect. It does not seem to increase risk-taking behavior. This means that cannabis rarely contributes to violence either to others or to oneself, whereas alcohol use is a major factor in deliberate self-harm, domestic accidents and violence."

 

 

Most recently, a logistical regression analysis of approximately 900 trauma patients published in the Journal of TRAUMA Injury, Infection, and Critical Care, determined that the use of cannabis is not independently associated with either violent or non-violent injuries requiring hospitalization. By contrast, alcohol and cocaine use are associated with violence-related injuries, the study found.
